headline: Three UK nations sign joint call for independence votes

sources.title: Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish leaders to sign independence pledge to pressure Westminster (ITV News)

chunks.text: On Monday, September 14, 2026, the first ministers of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland {{came together}} in Cardiff and {{signed off on}} a joint [[memorandum]]. All three lead parties that want their nations to {{break away}} from the United Kingdom. The document calls on the British government to "prepare, plan and facilitate" [[constitutional change]]. It {{spells out}} a demand for [[self-determination]]: the right to hold [[referendums]] on leaving.

verbs.correct: To meet as a group for a shared purpose
verbs.wrong: To slowly change your mind and agree
verbs.why: Neighbors come together after a storm to clean the street. The whole family comes together every Thanksgiving. The three first ministers came together in Cardiff to sign one joint document.

verbs.correct: To give formal approval to something
verbs.wrong: To add your name to a list of members
verbs.why: The boss signed off on the new budget this morning. A doctor must sign off on the plan before treatment starts. The three leaders signed off on a memorandum that asks London for the right to hold votes.

verbs.correct: To leave a group and become separate
verbs.wrong: To stop working because of a fault
verbs.why: Two members broke away from the club and started their own. A small region may try to break away from a larger country. All three parties in Cardiff want their nations to break away from the United Kingdom.

verbs.correct: To explain something in clear detail
verbs.wrong: To count the votes one by one
verbs.why: The contract spells out what each side must pay. Please spell out the rules so nobody is confused. The memorandum spells out a demand for the right to hold referendums on leaving.

chunks.text: The timing follows the May 2026 elections, when [[nationalist]] parties won control of all three [[devolved governments]] for the first time. In Wales, the winning party took 43 of 96 seats, ending a century of one party's [[dominance]]. In Scotland, the governing party stayed the largest and voted to {{push for}} a fresh independence vote. The first minister of Wales also {{brought up}} worries about [[fair funding]] from London.

verbs.correct: To try hard to make something happen
verbs.wrong: To delay something until a later time
verbs.why: Parents pushed for a new crosswalk near the school. The union is pushing for higher pay this year. In May, Scotland's governing party voted to push for a fresh independence vote.

verbs.correct: To mention a subject in a talk
verbs.wrong: To force a government to lose power
verbs.why: She brought up the parking problem at the meeting. Nobody wanted to bring up the cost of the trip. The first minister of Wales brought up worries about fair funding from London.

chunks.text: The British prime minister has {{ruled out}} any vote for now. On September 9 he told Parliament a Scottish referendum could {{go ahead}} with "clear consensus." One day later he {{walked back}} that remark in a letter to Scotland's first minister. A referendum, he wrote, is "[[off limits]]" before the next [[general election]]. There is no [[consensus]] in Scotland, and no clear [[majority]] in Northern Ireland wants to leave. A vote, he said, would {{get in the way of}} [[economic growth]].

verbs.correct: To say something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To give a final judgment in court
verbs.why: The coach ruled out a return before the final. Police have not ruled out a second suspect. The prime minister has ruled out any independence vote for now.

verbs.correct: To happen or start as planned
verbs.why: The concert will go ahead despite the rain. The sale went ahead after the bank approved the loan. On September 9 the prime minister said a Scottish referendum could go ahead with clear consensus.

verbs.correct: To withdraw a statement you made
verbs.wrong: To leave a meeting as a protest
verbs.why: The company walked back its promise of free delivery. He walked back the comment after the complaints. One day later the prime minister walked back his remark in a letter.

verbs.correct: To make progress on something harder
verbs.wrong: To avoid punishment for an action
verbs.why: Long meetings get in the way of real work. Do not let fear get in the way of your plans. The prime minister said a vote would get in the way of economic growth.

chunks.text: Scotland's first minister {{seized on}} the remark and said the [[momentum]] for independence is "undeniable." He said the prime minister could {{go down}} in history as the last leader of the United Kingdom. [[Unionist]] voices {{pushed back}}. The leader of Northern Ireland's largest unionist party said its people should decide the region's future. Downing Street said its position had not changed. The British government holds the [[legal power]] to allow a vote, so the memorandum {{comes down to}} [[political pressure]].

verbs.correct: To use a remark quickly to your advantage
verbs.why: Reporters seized on the minister's slip of the tongue. The lawyer seized on a small mistake in the report. Scotland's first minister seized on the prime minister's words about clear consensus.

verbs.correct: To be remembered in a certain way
verbs.why: That game will go down as the best final ever. She could go down as the school's greatest coach. Scotland's first minister said the prime minister could go down as the last leader of the United Kingdom.

verbs.correct: To argue against an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To continue with a plan despite problems
verbs.why: Staff pushed back when the new schedule was announced. Some parents pushed back against the longer school day. Unionist voices pushed back against the Cardiff memorandum.

verbs.correct: To depend mainly on one thing
verbs.wrong: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.why: In the end, the choice comes down to price. Winning often comes down to preparation. For now, the memorandum comes down to political pressure on London.

mainIdea.s: The first ministers of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland signed a joint memorandum asking London to allow independence votes. The prime minister says a referendum is off limits for now.
mainIdea.why: The three leaders signed the document in Cardiff on September 14, and the prime minister wrote that a referendum is off limits before the next general election.

mainIdea.s: The prime minister met the three first ministers in Cardiff and agreed to plan independence referendums. He said the votes could go ahead once Parliament finds a clear consensus.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the prime minister was not part of the meeting and did not agree to any vote. He walked back his remark and ruled out a referendum for now.

mainIdea.s: Scotland's parliament voted this week to hold an independence referendum next spring without London's approval. The prime minister has asked the courts to stop the vote before it happens.
mainIdea.why: No vote has been scheduled and no court case exists. The three leaders signed a memorandum that asks London to allow referendums.

tf.s: The three first ministers came together in Cardiff on September 14.
tf.why: They met in Cardiff on Monday, September 14, 2026, and signed off on a joint memorandum.

tf.s: The memorandum spells out a demand for the right to hold referendums.
tf.why: It asks the UK government to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change, including votes on leaving.

tf.s: The prime minister ruled out any independence vote before the next general election.
tf.why: In a letter to Scotland's first minister he wrote that a referendum is off limits for now.

tf.s: The prime minister walked back his remark in a letter two weeks later.
tf.why: He told Parliament on September 9 that a vote could go ahead with clear consensus, and he walked it back one day later.

tf.s: In May 2026, nationalist parties won control of two of the three devolved governments.
tf.why: For the first time, nationalist parties won control of all three, which is why the leaders are pushing for votes now.

tf.s: Downing Street said the prime minister's position had not changed.
tf.why: Unionist voices pushed back, and Downing Street said its position stayed the same.
